topics.title: Aviation weather requirements and minima
lesson: Aviation weather support turns observations and forecasts into go or no-go decisions. Legal minima come from the Canadian Aviation Regulations and operator procedures, so confirm them in official documents. The categories below come from the NAV CANADA guide and are not legal minima.

list: VFR: ceiling above 3,000 ft AGL and visibility above 5 SM.
MVFR (marginal VFR): ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft AGL or visibility 3 to 5 SM.
IFR: ceiling below 1,000 ft AGL or visibility below 3 SM (GFA IFR Outlook).
LIFR (low IFR): a US convention, ceiling below 500 ft and/or visibility below 1 SM. The NAV CANADA guide does not define LIFR for Canadian products.

lesson: The worse of the ceiling and visibility decides the category.

list: s. 602.114, controlled airspace: flight visibility not less than 3 miles, and at least 500 ft vertically and 1 mile horizontally from cloud. In a control zone, reported ground visibility must also be at least 3 miles and the aircraft at least 500 ft above the surface.
s. 602.115, uncontrolled airspace at or above 1,000 ft AGL: visibility 1 mile by day, 3 miles at night; at least 500 ft vertically and 2,000 ft horizontally from cloud.
Below 1,000 ft AGL in uncontrolled airspace, fixed-wing: visibility 2 miles by day, 3 at night, clear of cloud.
Pressure altitude: altitude above the standard datum plane of 1013.25 hPa, read when the altimeter is set to 29.92 inHg.

Density altitude: pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. Hot, high and humid days raise density altitude, which reduces engine power, lift and propeller efficiency. Takeoff rolls get longer and climb is poorer. NAV CANADA: a takeoff needing 1,000 ft at sea level needs about 2,000 ft at 5,000 ft operational altitude, and a METAR density altitude remark appears only when it is 200 ft or more above aerodrome elevation.

lesson.formula:
Crosswind = wind speed x sin(angle between wind and runway)
Headwind  = wind speed x cos(angle)

lesson: Example: 20 kt wind 30 degrees off the runway gives a 10 kt crosswind (20 x 0.5) and about 17 kt headwind. METAR winds are true, so convert to magnetic before comparing with the runway heading.

lesson.note: Different documents use different IFR/VFR thresholds. For automatic SPECIs, MANOBS 12.2.7 uses a 1,000 ft ceiling and 1 SM visibility as the IFR/VFR thresholds (plus 2,500 ft for ceiling and the aerodrome alternate minima), while the NAV CANADA GFA IFR Outlook uses below 1,000 ft or below 3 SM. Know which one a product uses.

Check the alternates and the forecast trend, not just the current report. Weather may drop below minima by arrival. For an alternate, a TAF with BECMG or TEMPO must meet alternate minima, while a PROB group need only meet landing minima (NAV CANADA guide).

terms: Lowest broken (5 to 7 oktas) or overcast (8 oktas) layer, or vertical visibility.
Pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature.
Part of the wind that blows across the runway.

questions.q: Using the NAV CANADA guide's flight categories, what is a ceiling of 800 ft with 5 SM visibility?
c: IFR
VFR
MVFR
LIFR
questions.e: IFR is a ceiling below 1,000 ft AGL or visibility below 3 SM. Either element is enough.

questions.q: A ceiling of 2,000 ft and visibility of 6 SM is:
c: MVFR
VFR
IFR
LIFR
questions.e: Ceilings of 1,000 to 3,000 ft are MVFR.

questions.q: What effect does a hot day have on density altitude?
c: It raises it, reducing aircraft performance
It lowers it, improving performance
No effect
It changes pressure altitude only
questions.e: Warmer air is less dense, so performance matches a higher altitude.

questions.q: Wind is 20 kt, 30 degrees off the runway heading. What is the approximate crosswind component?
c: 10 kt
17 kt
20 kt
5 kt
questions.e: Crosswind = 20 x sin 30 = 10 kt.

questions.q: Pressure altitude is read with the altimeter set to:
c: The current local QNH setting
The aerodrome QFE value
Zero inches of mercury
questions.e: Standard setting gives pressure altitude.

questions.q: Under CAR 602.114, what is the minimum flight visibility for VFR flight in controlled airspace?
c: 3 miles
1 mile
5 miles
1/4 mile
questions.e: CAR 602.114: flight visibility not less than 3 miles, with 500 ft vertical and 1 mile horizontal separation from cloud.

questions.q: Per the NAV CANADA guide, IFR on the GFA IFR Outlook means:
c: Ceiling below 1,000 ft AGL or visibility below 3 SM
Ceiling below 500 ft or visibility below 1 SM
Ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft or visibility 3 to 5 SM
Ceiling above 3,000 ft and visibility above 5 SM
questions.e: The GFA IFR Outlook gives less than 1,000 ft AGL or less than 3 SM. The 500 ft and 1 SM figures are the US LIFR category.

questions.q: An alternate airport is required when:
c: Forecast weather at destination is below specified minima
Weather at the destination is clear for the whole day
The flight takes place only at night
The pilot wants to land at a different airport
questions.e: Alternate rules apply when destination weather is marginal.

questions.q: A ceiling is defined as the lowest layer of:
c: Broken or overcast cloud, or vertical visibility
Few clouds only, with a base below 1,000 ft
Any cloud at all, including a thin layer of cirrus
Scattered cloud, up to half the sky covered
questions.e: Ceiling applies to BKN, OVC or obscuration.

questions.q: Pressure altitude is the altitude indicated when the altimeter is set to:
c: The local altimeter setting
The station pressure at the field
0.00 inHg
questions.e: Pressure altitude is read with the standard setting of 29.92 inHg.

questions.q: Density altitude increases when:
c: Temperature rises
Temperature falls
Humidity falls
Pressure rises
questions.e: Higher temperature thins the air and raises density altitude.

questions.q: When does a METAR density altitude remark appear, per the NAV CANADA guide?
c: Only when it is 200 ft or more above aerodrome elevation
Every report, whatever the value
Only when it is below sea level
Only on hot summer days
questions.e: NAV CANADA: the remark appears only when density altitude is 200 ft or more above aerodrome elevation.

questions.q: For an alternate, which TAF groups must meet alternate minima (NAV CANADA guide)?
c: BECMG and TEMPO groups
PROB groups only
No group; only the main body counts
FM groups only, never TEMPO
questions.e: NAV CANADA: BECMG and TEMPO must meet alternate minima; PROB conditions need only meet landing minima.

sources: NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): IFR, MVFR and VFR thresholds, LIFR not defined, oktas, density altitude, alternate rules for TAF groups, UTC
Canadian Aviation Regulations ss. 602.114 and 602.115: VFR visibility and cloud clearance
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 7.2.7 ceiling definition (lowest BKN or OVC layer, or vertical visibility)
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 12.2.7 (AUTO SPECI thresholds), 7.2.7 (ceiling)
unverified: Pressure altitude definition, crosswind and headwind trigonometry, and density altitude effects on engine power: standard aviation teaching, not on the pages read (the trigonometry was checked by arithmetic: 20 x sin 30 = 10, 20 x cos 30 = 17.3).
When an alternate is required (CAR 602.121 onward): not checked.
VFR minima above 1,000 ft AGL for special cases (helicopters, other airspace classes): not covered.

topics.title: Marine weather (sea state, swell, wind waves)
lesson: Marine forecasts matter for naval operations, small boats and offshore work. Waves depend on wind, but the pieces are different.

list: Wind waves (sea): generated by local wind. Steep, chaotic and short-period.
Swell: waves that have travelled out of the area where they formed. Longer period, smoother, and may arrive from storms hundreds or thousands of km away.

Significant wave height (Hs): average height of the highest one-third of waves. A good guide to what an observer reports as the typical wave height. The highest individual wave can be close to twice Hs.
Wave size depends on wind speed, duration (how long it has blown) and fetch (distance over open water).
Gale warning: winds of 34 to 47 kt, excluding gusts.
Storm warning: 48 to 63 kt, excluding gusts.
Hurricane force wind warning: 64 kt or more, excluding gusts. It does not mean a hurricane is expected.

lesson: The Beaufort scale (NWS) gives Force 8 (gale) 34 to 40 kt, Force 10 (storm) 48 to 55 kt and Force 12 (hurricane) 64 kt and above. ECCC also has a Strong Wind category; its threshold was not confirmed here.

list: Freezing spray: sea spray freezes on the vessel when air temperatures are below freezing, wind is strong and the sea is cold. Ice builds quickly on rigging and superstructure and reduces stability. Seen on Atlantic Canada waters in winter.
Fog: advection fog is common off Nova Scotia and the Grand Banks.
Waves steepen when wind blows against a strong current or tide, creating rips.

lesson.note: Shorter-period swell with high waves is harder on small boats than longer-period swell of the same height.

terms: Distance of open water over which wind blows.
Waves that have moved away from their generating area.
Mean height of the highest third of waves.
Sea spray that freezes on contact with a vessel.

questions.q: How does swell differ from wind waves?
c: Swell has travelled away from the source area and is longer-period and more regular
Swell is generated by the local wind and is shorter-period and more chaotic
Swell only occurs in winter and is always larger than any wind wave
Swell is caused by tides and its height is set by the depth of the water
questions.e: Swell is organised by travel away from the storm that generated it.

questions.q: Significant wave height is:
c: The mean of the highest one-third of waves
The height of the single largest wave in the record
The average height of every wave in the record
The wave height measured at the shoreline only
questions.e: Hs is a standard statistic and approximates visual estimates of wave height.

questions.q: Which three factors determine wind wave size?
c: Wind speed, duration and fetch
Water depth, temperature and salinity
Moon phase, tide and current
Pressure, humidity and visibility
questions.e: Stronger, longer wind over more open water produces larger waves.

questions.q: What wind speeds does a marine gale warning cover?
c: 34 to 47 kt
20 to 33 kt
48 to 63 kt
64 kt or more
questions.e: Gale 34 to 47 kt, storm 48 to 63 kt, hurricane force 64 kt or more.

questions.q: What conditions favour freezing spray?
c: Below-freezing air, strong wind and cold sea water
Warm air with calm seas and warm surface water
Heavy rain with warm sea water and light winds
Light winds and fog over water above 10 C
questions.e: Spray freezes when it hits a vessel in sub-freezing air.

questions.q: Wind waves are generated by:
c: Local wind blowing over the sea surface
Earthquakes under the sea floor, travelling as long waves
Distant storms only, many days away from the coast
The gravitational pull of the moon and the sun on the sea
questions.e: Waves caused by local wind are wind waves.

questions.q: Swell is:
c: Waves that have travelled out of their generating area
Locally generated short waves with sharp, breaking crests
Tidal waves driven by the moon's pull on the sea
Waves that break onto the shore with surf and foam
questions.e: Swell has longer periods and smooth crests.

questions.q: Wave height increases with:
c: Wind speed, duration and fetch
Air pressure, humidity and cloud cover over the sea
Water temperature, salinity and the depth of the ocean
Tide level, moon phase and coastal geography only
questions.e: These three factors set the fully developed sea.

questions.q: A 34 kt wind on the Beaufort scale is force:
c: 8 (gale)
questions.e: Beaufort 8 is 34 to 40 kt.

questions.q: In marine forecasts, storm warnings are generally for winds of:
c: 48 to 63 kt
10 to 15 kt
20 to 25 kt
34 to 47 kt
questions.e: Storm force winds are 48 to 63 kt; gale warnings cover 34 to 47 kt.

questions.q: Wave period is:
c: Time between successive crests
The height from a trough to the next crest of a wave
The wind speed measured at the buoy site in knots
The tide level at the nearest port at high water
questions.e: Period is measured in seconds between crests.

questions.q: Does an ECCC hurricane force wind warning mean a hurricane is expected?
c: No; it means winds of 64 kt or more, excluding gusts
Yes; a hurricane is forecast to arrive
Yes, but only over open ocean
Only if the pressure is below 960 hPa
questions.e: ECCC: a Hurricane Force Wind Warning does not suggest that a hurricane is expected.

sources: ECCC, Canadian marine warning program, chapter 1: gale, storm and hurricane force thresholds, excluding gusts
NWS Portland, Beaufort scale: Force 8, 10 and 12 ranges
Significant wave height article: mean of the highest third (H1/3), matches mariner estimates, largest waves about double Hs
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): Table 3-1 (Beaufort scale: force 8 gale 34 to 40 kt, force 10 storm 48 to 55, force 12 hurricane 64 or more)
unverified: Freezing spray criteria and conditions: not on the ECCC page read. Atlantic Canada winter occurrence is not confirmed.
Swell versus wind waves, fetch and duration, wave steepening against a current, and the claim about shorter-period swell: standard teaching, not confirmed.

topics.title: Weather effects on military operations
lesson: Weather affects every environment. A weather technician's job is to turn the forecast into impacts for the commander. Use only unclassified, open information in this study repository.

list: Cloud and visibility: limit flying, air support, visual reconnaissance and ISR. Fog and low cloud also slow ground and sea movement.
Wind: affects aircraft handling, helicopter and parachute operations, small-boat work, and smoke and obscurant use. Strong wind also affects shooting accuracy.
Temperature: cold brings frostbite, hypothermia and equipment problems. Heat brings heat injury and increased water needs. Humidex and wind chill help estimate personnel risk.
Precipitation: reduces visibility, softens ground (trafficability), raises river levels, and affects equipment and comms.
Sea state: limits small boat launch and recovery, replenishment at sea, and helicopter deck operations.
Illumination: moon phase and cloud cover determine night vision goggle performance.
ECCC humidex: 30 to 39 some discomfort, 40 to 45 great discomfort (avoid exertion), over 45 dangerous (heat stroke possible). Wind chill levels are in the Severe weather lesson.

lesson: Release of smoke, chemical or biological agents, or other contaminants depends on wind and stability. In stable conditions (a surface inversion on a clear, calm night) the plume stays close to the ground, concentrations stay high, and the downwind hazard area is long. Unstable daytime conditions mix and dilute the material faster.
Operational impact tables convert weather values into green, amber or red thresholds for each activity. The forecast should state the relevant element, the threshold, the timing and the confidence.

lesson.note: The best brief answers: what is it, when, how bad, how confident, and what decision does it affect.

terms: Ability of terrain to support vehicles.
Natural light available, mainly moon and cloud, which affects night vision devices.
Resistance of the atmosphere to vertical mixing.

questions.q: Which conditions limit the dispersion of a ground-level release, keeping concentrations high near the ground?
c: Stable conditions such as a surface inversion
Strong daytime heating and vigorous vertical mixing
Unstable air with gusty winds and deep convection
A deep, well-mixed layer with strong turbulence
questions.e: Stability suppresses vertical mixing so the plume stays low and concentrated.

questions.q: What does night vision goggle performance mostly depend on?
c: Available natural illumination from moon phase and cloud
Surface wind speed and the direction of the wind
Relative humidity and the dew point at the surface
Atmospheric pressure and its change over three hours
questions.e: Image intensifiers need ambient light, which depends on moon and cloud.

questions.q: How does precipitation commonly affect ground operations?
c: It softens ground and reduces trafficability
It improves visibility and hardens the terrain surface
It has little effect on movement across open ground
It increases the range of night vision devices
questions.e: Wet ground slows vehicles and can bog them down.

questions.q: What does low cloud and fog most directly limit?
c: Visual flying, air support and visual ISR
Radio line of sight and satellite communications
Barometer readings and altimeter settings
GPS accuracy and position fixing for ground units
questions.e: Ceiling and visibility drive flight and visual observation limits.

questions.q: What should an operational weather impact statement include?
c: The element, threshold, timing and confidence
The model name and the run time of the guidance
Only the forecast air temperature at the base
A chart image with no description of the impacts
questions.e: A clear impact statement ties a weather element to a decision threshold and expected time.

questions.q: Low cloud and fog most affect which military operation?
c: Air operations and flying
Ship refits in harbour, where weather has little effect
Rifle drills on a range with fixed targets and no wind
Administrative work done in a heated office building
questions.e: Ceilings and visibility restrict aircraft operations.

questions.q: Extreme cold affects personnel through:
c: Frostbite and hypothermia risk
Dehydration and sunburn, with no effect on circulation
Overheating and heat exhaustion in light clothing
Eye strain only, with no effect on skin or body core
questions.e: Wind chill increases exposure risk.

questions.q: Wind chill is a measure of:
c: How cold the exposed skin feels
The actual air temperature measured in a Stevenson screen
The relative humidity of the air at the surface
The atmospheric pressure at the exposed location
questions.e: It combines wind and temperature.

questions.q: Heat stress is assessed using:
c: Humidex or WBGT
Barometer
Anemometer
Visibility
questions.e: Heat and humidity indexes show risk.

questions.q: Why is wind important for NBC and smoke operations?
c: It determines the transport and dispersion of plumes
It changes the pressure of the air and so the plume density
It changes the humidity and so the visibility only
It has no effect on the movement of smoke or plumes
questions.e: Plume movement follows the wind.

questions.q: Fog may help or hinder operations because:
c: It reduces visibility for both sides
It increases visibility for both sides in equal measure
It has no effect on observation, navigation or concealment
It improves radar performance for the forces on the ground
questions.e: Reduced visibility affects observation, navigation and concealment.

questions.q: What does an ECCC humidex above 45 indicate?
c: Dangerous; heat stroke possible
Little discomfort
Some discomfort
Great discomfort with no real danger
questions.e: ECCC: 20-29 little discomfort, 30-39 some discomfort, 40-45 great discomfort and avoid exertion, above 45 dangerous with heat stroke possible.

sources: ECCC, How to use the Humidex: ranges and wording
ECCC, Wind Chill Index: see the Severe weather lesson
unverified: Operational impacts by element, dispersion and stability, night vision illumination, and green/amber/red impact tables: general military meteorology teaching with no public source read. Check against unclassified doctrine you are authorised to use.
WBGT as a heat stress measure: not checked.

topics.title: Briefing structure and delivery
lesson: A good weather brief is short, relevant and actionable. It answers what the commander or pilot needs to decide.

list: Bottom line up front: the key impact and recommendation in the first sentence or two.
Situation: the large-scale pattern, in a few lines.
Forecast: by time period for the area of operations. State the elements that matter.
Impacts: connect the weather to the operation, using thresholds.
Hazards and risks: warnings, watches, and the trigger conditions.
Confidence and alternatives: how sure you are and what could change.
Next update: when you will brief again.
Use UTC (Zulu) time, or state the zone clearly, to avoid confusion. METAR, TAF and PIREP times are in UTC with a Z suffix (NAV CANADA guide). Give local time as well when the audience needs it.
Use numbers with units, thresholds and times. 'Winds 20 gusting 30 kt from the west from 1800Z' beats 'windy later'.
Show one clear graphic where it helps. Do not read the slide.
Say what you do not know. State confidence in plain terms.
Give the valid time of the data and its source.
Answer the question asked. Keep detailed science for questions.

lesson: Brief proactively when conditions change from what was briefed. Note what changed and why.

lesson.note: If the audience remembers one thing, it should be the decision-relevant message.

terms: Statement of how likely the forecast is to verify.

questions.q: What does BLUF stand for?
c: Bottom line up front
Briefing line under forecast
Best local update forecast
Basic layout of urgent facts
questions.e: BLUF means lead with the key message and recommendation.

questions.q: Why use UTC (Zulu) in weather briefs?
c: It avoids time zone confusion
It is easier to read
It is local time everywhere
It adjusts for daylight saving
questions.e: A single reference time prevents mistakes across zones.

questions.q: Which is the better forecast statement?
c: West winds 20 gusting 30 kt from 1800Z
Windy conditions are expected later in the day
Winds will probably increase at some point soon
It should be breezy once the front goes through
questions.e: Specific values, direction and time make the statement useful.

questions.q: How should uncertainty be handled in a brief?
c: State confidence and what could change the forecast
Leave it out so the brief sounds clear and decisive
Add extra charts to cover over any areas of doubt
Quote the model name and avoid any further comment
questions.e: Decision makers need to know how much to trust the forecast.

questions.q: What should a briefing focus on?
c: Decision-relevant impacts
All available data
Every model run
Historical weather trivia
questions.e: The brief exists to support a decision.

questions.q: A weather briefing should begin with:
c: The synoptic situation or the critical weather for the user
Details of historical data from the last thirty years
Model biases and the limitations of each forecast product
Pleasantries and a long description of the local climate
questions.e: Start with the big picture or the user's key concern.

questions.q: In a briefing, uncertainty should be:
c: Stated clearly with confidence levels
Hidden, so the briefing sounds more certain to the user
Ignored, so the user hears only the most likely outcome
Exaggerated, so the user plans for the worst case always
questions.e: Decision makers need to know confidence.

questions.q: The BLUF principle means:
c: Bottom line up front
Briefing later until finished
Basic local update form
Brief low, urgent first
questions.e: Give the key message first.

questions.q: A good weather briefing ends with:
c: Impact on the mission and questions
A long data dump of every model run available
A list of the sources used and the time of issue
A random fact about the weather in the area
questions.e: Link the weather to decisions.

questions.q: Which should be included for a flight briefing?
c: Winds aloft, icing, turbulence, cloud and visibility along the route
Only the surface temperature at the departure airport
Only the time of sunrise at the destination field
Only the rainfall totals for the last twenty-four hours
questions.e: Route weather hazards are central.

questions.q: When the forecast changes after a briefing, the briefer should:
c: Update the user promptly
Wait for the next day
Ignore the change
Delete the briefing
questions.e: Changes that affect the mission must be passed on.

sources: NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): METAR, TAF and PIREP times in UTC with Z
unverified: The BLUF structure and delivery habits are briefing practice, not a published standard I could cite. Check your unit's briefing SOP.
No public Canadian source for the briefing format was found.

topics.title: Climatology of the Atlantic region
lesson: Atlantic Canada has a maritime climate with strong influence from the ocean, but it is also exposed to continental air. Knowing the regional patterns helps you spot what is unusual.

list: Prevailing flow: westerly, so weather arrives mostly from the west. Cold continental air crosses the region in winter. The ocean moderates temperature, giving milder winters and cooler summers than the interior at the same latitude, especially on the coast.
Storm tracks: winter lows move up the coast or across from the Great Lakes. Nor'easters bring heavy snow, wind and coastal flooding. Rain, snow and freezing rain often mix in the same storm.

Freezing rain: most often observed in eastern Canada including the Atlantic provinces, with the St. Lawrence valley a hotspot (ClimateData.ca). Warm moist air overrunning cold air near the coast is the usual mechanism (not confirmed for Atlantic Canada specifically).

Tropical cyclones: the season runs 1 June to 30 November and ECCC says August and September have the most storms in Atlantic Canada. Atlantic Canada is the most exposed region. Since 1950, 30 hurricanes or strong post-tropical storms have hit land in Canada, about one every 2 to 3 years. Examples: Juan (2003, Halifax), Igor (2010, a Category 1 hurricane in Newfoundland) and Fiona (2022, eastern Nova Scotia, the most damaging storm of any kind in Atlantic Canadian history, over $800 million insured damage).
Fog: very common off Nova Scotia and over the Grand Banks, where warm Gulf Stream air meets the cold Labrador Current. Sea fog is most frequent in spring and summer.
Spring: late and cool near the coast because of cold water. Sea breezes and fog are common.
Autumn: the ocean is at its warmest. Tropical remnants and strong lows increase windy, wet days.

lesson: Local knowledge improves forecasts. For example, when the model shows a warm southerly flow over the cold coastal water, expect fog and low cloud even if the model does not show it clearly. When a coastal low tracks slightly west, rain replaces snow along the coast.

lesson.note: Study actual cases. Pull up past storms (for example from ECCC archives) and compare what was forecast with what happened.

terms: Cold ocean current flowing south along the Labrador and Newfoundland coasts.
Warm Atlantic current flowing northeast off the US east coast.
Climate moderated by a nearby large body of water.

questions.q: Why is the Grand Banks region so foggy?
c: Warm Gulf Stream air flows over the cold Labrador Current
Cold continental air flows across the warm Gulf Stream
Frequent thunderstorms form along the shore all year
Persistent high pressure keeps the region calm and humid
questions.e: Warm moist air cooling over cold water produces advection fog.

questions.q: When do most tropical cyclone impacts occur in Atlantic Canada, per ECCC?
c: August and September
December to February
March to April
May to June
questions.e: ECCC: the season is 1 June to 30 November and August and September have the most storms in Atlantic Canada.

questions.q: What is a typical winter storm track bringing heavy snow and strong northeast winds to the Maritimes?
c: A nor'easter along the US east coast
A tropical depression from the Pacific
A monsoon
A polar high
questions.e: Coastal lows that deepen off the US east coast produce nor'easters.

questions.q: Why are Atlantic Canada's winters milder than the continental interior at the same latitude?
c: Ocean moderation
Lack of cold air
Higher elevation
Constant south winds
questions.e: The ocean's heat capacity moderates temperature swings.

questions.q: Why is freezing rain common in Atlantic Canada?
c: Warm moist air often overrides sub-freezing air near the coast
Mountains force air upward and freeze rain at high elevation
Summer heat leaves most of the soil colder than the air
Fronts do not form in the region, so the air stays uniform
questions.e: Warm air aloft over a shallow cold layer at the surface produces freezing rain.

questions.q: Fog is most common on the Atlantic coast in:
c: Late spring and summer
Midwinter
Late autumn only
Never
questions.e: Warm moist air over cold water gives advection fog.

questions.q: Nova Scotia gets its coldest temperatures typically in:
c: January and February
June and July, when the sea is at its warmest
August, when the days are long and winds are light
October, when the first gales cross the Atlantic
questions.e: Winter minima occur in these months.

questions.q: The Labrador Current influences the region by:
c: Bringing cold water south
Bringing warm water north
Having no effect
Stopping storms
questions.e: It cools coastal waters and increases fog.

questions.q: Nor'easters are most frequent in:
c: Winter
Summer
Spring only
None of the seasons
questions.e: Intense coastal lows affect the region from late autumn to early spring.

questions.q: Hurricane season in the Atlantic is:
c: June 1 to November 30
January to March
December to February
July only
questions.e: Official Atlantic season dates.

questions.q: The Gulf Stream influences the region by:
c: Warm water that fuels storm intensification and fog contrasts
Carries ice south and cools the coastal waters in spring
Cools the coast and so stops fog from forming offshore
Has no effect on storms, fog or sea surface temperatures
questions.e: Warm water meeting cold shelf water creates sharp contrasts.

sources: ECCC, Hurricanes: frequently asked questions: season dates, August and September most storms, Atlantic Canada most exposed, Juan, Igor and Fiona
ClimateData.ca, Freezing rain and climate change: freezing rain most often in eastern Canada, St. Lawrence valley hotspot
unverified: Prevailing westerlies, ocean moderation, nor'easter tracks, coldest months, Grand Banks fog and the Gulf Stream and Labrador Current contrast, spring and autumn descriptions: general climatology, not checked against ECCC climate normals.
The earlier claim that peak tropical risk is mid-September was removed (ECCC says August and September).
The earlier claim that Atlantic Canada has one of the highest freezing rain frequencies in Canada was softened.
